title: straight_fantasy
caption:
You're straight. And you've had a same-sex fantasy. You're far from alone. 🌈

Researchers asked over 1,500 adults about their fantasies. 85% of them were straight.

Women: 37% had fantasized about sex with a woman. Men: 21%. One in five.

Yet only 6% of the women, and under 2% of the men, said they were gay.

So a fantasy isn't a label. It's just a fantasy.

No label needed. Just save it. 🔖

Not just you (One online survey in Quebec, Canada. The percentages are for the whole sample, which was mostly but not only straight.)

Source: Joyal, Cossette & Lapierre (2015), "What Exactly Is an Unusual Sexual Fantasy?", Journal of Sexual Medicine

title: wedding_cost
caption:
The more you spend on your wedding, the more likely the divorce. Seriously. 💍

Wedding Math, part 1/3. Two economists asked over 3,000 Americans who had been married: what did your wedding cost? And did the marriage last?

Women whose wedding cost over $20,000 had 1.6× the divorce risk of those who spent $5,000–10,000. Men who spent under $1,000 had about half the risk.

Why? Nobody knows for sure. The researchers' guess: debt. And money stress is relationship stress.

How much would you spend on your wedding? 👇

Part 2 tomorrow: the ring.

Not just you (It's a link, not proof: a survey shows a correlation, not the cause.)

Source: Francis-Tan & Mialon (2015), "'A Diamond is Forever' and Other Fairy Tales: The Relationship between Wedding Expenses and Marriage Duration", Economic Inquiry

title: mixed_signals
caption:
She smiled. So she's into you? Maybe not. 😶

About 200 students went speed dating, then rated how interested each partner was in them. Men tended to overestimate women's sexual interest. Women tended to underestimate men's.

The worst readers: men looking for something casual, and men who were most attracted to her.

The more you want it, the worse you read it. So ask. Don't guess. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Perilloux, Easton & Buss (2012), Psychological Science

Send this to the friend who "just knows" 👀

title: ring_guests
caption:
The size of your wedding is linked to your divorce risk. 🤔

Wedding Math, part 2/3. Plot twist: big wins. But only if it's big in the right way.

In the same survey of over 3,000 Americans who had been married, the more guests came, the lower the divorce risk, up to about 200 people.

But the ring? Men who spent $2,000–4,000 had 1.3× the divorce risk of those who spent $500–2,000. And couples who took a honeymoon were less likely to divorce.

So spend less on the ring. And invite more people.

Big wedding or small: what did yours look like? 👇

Part 3 tomorrow: the age gap.

Not just you (It's a link, not proof: a survey shows a correlation, not the cause.)

Source: Francis-Tan & Mialon (2015), "'A Diamond is Forever' and Other Fairy Tales: The Relationship between Wedding Expenses and Marriage Duration", Economic Inquiry

title: desire_gap
caption:
You want it more than your partner. Or less. Most couples know this. 💞

In one study, 80% remembered a recent time their desire didn't match their partner's.

So researchers followed couples for three weeks. Every day, both partners rated their desire.

What helped: caring about each other's needs. People who wanted their partner to feel loved were more open, even when they weren't in the mood. And both partners were happier.

But only when it was free. Out of guilt or pressure, it doesn't work. And a no gets accepted.

So it's not about who's right. It's about caring. Both ways.

Send this to your partner. 👇

Not just you (Three studies from one lab. A link, not proof. Consent first, always.)

Source: Day, Muise, Joel & Impett (2015), "To Do It or Not to Do It? How Communally Motivated People Navigate Sexual Interdependence Dilemmas", Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

title: age_gap
caption:
Your age gap is linked to your divorce risk. Here's the math! 💞

Wedding Math, part 3/3. Same survey, over 3,000 Americans who had been married. Compared with couples the same age:

1 year apart: 3% more likely to divorce.
5 years: 18%.
10 years: 39%.

So love has no age. But statistics do.

What's your age gap? 👇

Not just you (It's a link, not proof: a survey shows a correlation, not the cause. And plenty of couples with a big gap last.)

Source: Francis-Tan & Mialon (2015), "'A Diamond is Forever' and Other Fairy Tales: The Relationship between Wedding Expenses and Marriage Duration", Economic Inquiry

title: disgust
caption:
Why isn't it gross? Think about it. 🪲

90 women watched one of three films: erotica, extreme sports, or a train ride. Then came the gross part: drink from a cup with a bug in it, handle a condom that looked used (all fake, all clean).

The aroused group found the sexual tasks less disgusting, and was more willing to do them.

Arousal turns the disgust dial down. Otherwise, intimacy would be pretty hard to go through with. So if things feel weird afterwards? That's just the dial turning back up. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Borg & de Jong (2012), PLoS ONE

Never thought about it like that? 👇

title: blind_day
caption:
A dating site turned off every photo. For one day. 🙈

On "Love Is Blind Day", OkCupid hid all pictures for seven hours. People answered first messages 44% more often, and conversations went deeper.

Then, at 4 p.m., the photos came back. About 2,200 conversations had started blind. They just melted away.

Without a face, we were kinder. With one, we got picky.

Would you date blind? 👇

Not just you · Platform data (OkCupid, not a peer-reviewed study)

Source: Christian Rudder, "We Experiment On Human Beings!", OkCupid blog (2014) · book: Dataclysm (2014)

title: bedtimes
caption:
You and your partner go to bed at different times. That costs more than sleep. 🌙

A study compared 150 couples: morning people, night owls, and mixed pairs.

The mismatched couples had more conflict. Less serious talk. Less time together. And less sex.

A newer study tracked couples with sleep sensors. When wives were happier with the marriage, the couple slept more in sync.

You don't have to be the same type. One idea: go to bed together. The night owl can get up again.

Who's the night owl? 👇

Not just you (Both studies show a link, not proof: unhappy couples may also drift apart at night. The first study is from 1991. Going to bed together is an idea, not something these studies tested.)

Sources: Larson, Crane & Smith (1991), "Morning and Night Couples", Journal of Marital and Family Therapy · Gunn et al. (2015), "Sleep Concordance in Couples Is Associated with Relationship Characteristics", Sleep

title: friend_hours
caption:
You just moved, and making friends feels slow. Here's the real math. ⏳

A researcher surveyed 355 adults who had just moved and followed 112 new college students for weeks.

From stranger to casual friend: about 50 hours.
To real friend: about 90.
To close friend: over 200 hours.

That's months of showing up. If it's not clicking yet: it's not you, it's the hours.

Who's your 200-hour friend? 👇

Not just you (Estimates from surveys of people making new friends.)

Source: Hall (2019), "How many hours does it take to make a friend?", Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

title: kissing
caption:
Kissing is human nature. Right? 💋

Anthropologists looked at 168 cultures around the world. Romantic kissing showed up in fewer than half.

Every culture they studied in the Middle East did it. In South America, only 4 out of 33. And among hunter-gatherers, there was little sign of it at all.

So the kiss isn't universal. It's culture. Which makes it a little more special. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Jankowiak, Volsche & Garcia (2015), American Anthropologist

Did you know this? Tell me in the comments.

title: live
caption:
This video tracks you, live. ⏱️

Seconds 1–3: you decide. Swipe or stay.
Seconds 4–7: the hook is done. Now the video has to pay off.

Tests for Facebook found people remember a feed post after just 0.25 seconds. And up to 47% of a video ad's impact lands in the first 3 seconds.

The median YouTube Short is watched about 45% through. If you reached the end, you're way past that.

Instagram says its top three ranking signals are watch time, likes and sends. You just gave the first one.

The other two? You know what to do. 👇

Not just you. (Industry data; the curve in the video is schematic.)

Sources: Fors Marsh for Facebook (2016) · Facebook/Nielsen · quso.ai Shorts benchmark · Adam Mosseri, Instagram (2025)

title: friend_envy
caption:
Your friend's success stings. That doesn't make you a bad friend. 🫣

In a classic experiment, men brought a friend to a word-guessing game. They could give easy clues or hard ones.

Then the researchers said the game measured intelligence. And they gave their friend harder clues than a stranger. In 10 of 13 sessions.

When it's not your thing, you cheer for your friend. When it is your thing, their win can feel like your loss.

What helps: celebrate anyway. In studies on good news, an excited, curious reply went with closer relationships.

So feel the sting. Then say: tell me everything.

Tag a friend you're proud of. 👇

Not just you (The 1980 experiment was small and only included men. When the game was described as unimportant, friends got the easier clues. The good-news studies show a link, not proof.)

Sources: Tesser & Smith (1980), "Some Effects of Task Relevance and Friendship on Helping", Journal of Experimental Social Psychology · Gable, Reis, Impett & Asher (2004), "What Do You Do When Things Go Right?", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

title: liking_gap
caption:
After a first conversation, people like you more than you think. Seriously. 🙂

Researchers paired strangers for a five-minute chat. Then both rated: how much do I like them? And how much do they like me?

People underestimated how much they were liked. Even in longer conversations. And among college roommates, the gap lasted for months.

So that awkward chat? It went better than you think.

Send this to someone you just met. 👇

Not just you (Five studies.)

Source: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018), "The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think?", Psychological Science

title: afterplay
caption:
The most underrated part of intimacy? What happens after. 🫶

Researchers surveyed over 300 people, then followed 101 couples for three weeks. On average, people spent about 15 minutes on affection afterwards: cuddling, kissing, talking.

The longer that lasted, the more satisfied people were, with their sex life and with their relationship. Three months later, they were still more satisfied. And for parents, the link was even stronger.

So don't rush off. The cuddle counts. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Muise, Giang & Impett (2014), Archives of Sexual Behavior

Tag someone who needs to stay a little longer 😉

title: split_opinion
caption:
Want more messages? Then not everyone should like your looks. 💌

On a dating site, men rated how attractive women looked, from 1 to 5.

Two women, same average: 3.
Left: almost everyone says 3.
Right: people say 1, or 5.

Women like her got far more messages. In one example, 3x as many.

Why? If some men aren't into her, others expect less competition.

So don't try to please everyone. Lean into what makes you different. ✨

Not just you (OkCupid platform data from 2011, not peer-reviewed. Men rating women only. The dots in the video are a schematic example.)

Source: OkTrends, "The Mathematics Of Beauty" (2011)

title: afterglow
caption:
One good night together keeps working for two whole days. ✨

214 newlywed couples kept a diary for two weeks, every single night. After intimacy, satisfaction stayed higher for about 48 hours. That held for men and women, younger and older.

And couples with a stronger afterglow were happier months later. Their satisfaction dropped less over time.

So it's not just one night. It's a two-day glow. Worth keeping warm. 🧡

Not just you · After Dark

Source: Meltzer et al. (2017), Psychological Science

Tag your person 🔥

title: apology
caption:
Most apologies miss the most important part! 🙏

Researchers tested six parts of an apology with over 700 people.

Number one: own it. "This was my fault."
Number two: offer to fix it.
The least useful part: asking for forgiveness.

So: own it. Fix it. Don't beg.

Save this for your next sorry. 👇

Not just you (Survey experiments with 755 people.)

Source: Lewicki, Polin & Lount (2016), "An Exploration of the Structure of Effective Apologies", Negotiation and Conflict Management Research

title: casual
caption:
Who's really on dating apps just for hookups? 🔥

On OkCupid, users could tick what they're looking for. One option: casual sex.

Straight men: 6.1%
Gay men and lesbians: 6.9%
Straight women: 0.8%

One in 16 men. One in 125 women. At least, that's what they were willing to tick. 😏

Not just you · After Dark (Platform data, self-reported)

Source: Christian Rudder, Dataclysm (2014)

title: old_photo
caption:
That hot profile photo? It's probably old. 📸

OkCupid compared what users claim with what its data shows. People are about two inches shorter than they say. And 20% poorer.

But the best part: over a third of the hottest photos were at least a year old. Hot photos were more than twice as likely to be 3+ years old (12% vs 5%).

So the better the photo, the older it probably is. 👀

Not just you · Platform data (OkCupid, 2010, not peer-reviewed)

Source: OkTrends, "The Big Lies People Tell In Online Dating" (2010)

title: onlyfans
caption:
OnlyFans paid its creators $6.3 billion last year. So is everyone on there rich? 💸

Since 2016 it has paid out $30 billion, and 5,076 creators have made over a million.

But there are about 2.5 million active creators. Spread the money evenly and each gets roughly $2,500 a year, about $200 a month. And it isn't spread evenly: one analyst estimates the top 10% take about three quarters of it.

The money is real. It's just very, very concentrated. 📊

Surprised? 👇

Not just you · After Dark (Platform data; the average is our own calculation, the top-10% share is an analyst estimate)

Source: OnlyFans figures via Tubefilter (Aug 2026) · Matthew Ball, "Breaking Down OnlyFans' Stunning Economics"

title: joint_account
caption:
Couples who shared one bank account stayed happier. And that's an experiment. 💳

Researchers took 230 engaged or newly married couples with separate accounts and randomly told them: merge, stay separate, or do whatever you want.

Over two years, couples with separate accounts became less happy with their relationship. Couples with a joint account didn't. And they felt more in sync about money.

So love is shared. Maybe money too.

Joint or separate? 👇

Not just you (Not for every couple: the researchers say it may not suit insecure relationships or finances.)

Source: Olson, Rick, Small & Finkel (2023), "Common Cents: Bank Account Structure and Couples' Relationship Dynamics", Journal of Consumer Research

title: beer
caption:
One question on your first date tells you how the night ends. 🍺

"Do you like the taste of beer?"

Beer fans were 60% more likely to be okay sleeping with someone they just met. Men and women.

Want something long-term instead? Ask three things:
1. Do you like horror movies?
2. Have you ever traveled alone to another country?
3. Would it be fun to quit everything and live on a sailboat?

32% of long-term couples agreed on all three. Almost 4x more often than chance.

Your answers? 👇

Not just you · After Dark (Platform data, OkCupid 2011, a correlation, not a rule)

Source: OkTrends, "The Best Questions For A First Date" (2011)

title: bio
caption:
You spent an hour on your dating bio. Nobody read it. ✍️

OkCupid had people rate profiles for looks and personality. Some saw the text, some saw only the photo. The scores barely moved: your text made up less than 10% of what people thought of you.

And looks versus personality? For 92% of profiles, the two scores were almost the same. 😬

So your words matter. Your photo just talks louder.

Not just you · Platform experiment (OkCupid, not peer-reviewed)

Source: Christian Rudder, "We Experiment On Human Beings!", OkCupid blog (2014)

title: below_average
caption:
Women rated 80% of men as below average. 😳

OkCupid analyzed how its users rated each other's looks. Women were harsh: 80% of men landed below medium. Men rated women on a fair curve, most women right in the middle.

But men's messages? Two thirds went to the best-looking third of women.

So women judge harder. Men chase harder.

Which one is worse? 👇

Not just you · Platform data (OkCupid, 2009, not peer-reviewed)

Source: OkTrends, "Your Looks and Your Inbox" (2009)

title: social_cap
caption:
Quick guess: how much social media a day made students less lonely? 📱

Not zero. 143 students, three weeks. Half used Facebook, Instagram and Snapchat as usual. The other half: 10 minutes per app per day. 30 minutes total.

Their loneliness dropped. Depression too.

So you don't have to quit. Just cap it.

What's your screen time? 👇

Not just you (One experiment with college students.)

Source: Hunt, Marx, Lipson & Young (2018), "No More FOMO: Limiting Social Media Decreases Loneliness and Depression", Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology

title: fake_match
caption:
What if your perfect match is a lie? 💔

OkCupid took pairs who were a bad match, just 30%, and told them they were 90%. They messaged more. And they acted like a good match, even though they weren't.

The site's own verdict: "the mere myth of compatibility works just as well as the truth."

When OkCupid admitted it in 2014, users were furious.

So maybe chemistry is partly what you're told to expect. 🧪

Not just you · Platform experiment (OkCupid, not peer-reviewed)

Source: Christian Rudder, "We Experiment On Human Beings!", OkCupid blog (2014)

title: slop
caption:
Think you can spot AI slop? Most people can't. 🤖

11,000 people took an online test: 50 pictures, human or AI? The median score was 60%. Pure guessing gets you 50.

The most liked picture in the whole test? Made by AI. Even people who said they hate AI art put AI pieces in half of their top ten.

So maybe we don't hate slop. We hate knowing it's slop. 🫠

Not just you. (Online survey of blog readers, not peer-reviewed.)

Source: Scott Alexander, "How Did You Do On The AI Art Turing Test?", Astral Codex Ten (2024)

PS: This video was made with code. Did that change how you feel about it? 👇

title: forever_20
caption:
A 20-year-old man finds 20-year-old women most attractive. So does a 50-year-old man. 😬

On OkCupid, men of every age rated women in their early 20s highest. Women's taste grew up with them: their ideal age rose with their own.

But here's the twist: men mostly messaged women close to their own age.

So men's ratings say one thing. Their messages say another.

Not just you · Platform data (OkCupid, not peer-reviewed)

Source: Christian Rudder, Dataclysm (2014)

title: sleep_fights
caption:
Bad sleep makes couples fight more. That's science! 😴

You're not imagining it. Berkeley psychologists asked people in relationships to track their sleep and their fights for two weeks.

After a bad night, they had more conflict the next day. Even good sleepers. And in the lab, tired couples were worse at reading each other's feelings.

So before the big talk: sleep on it. Literally.

Send this to your tired partner. 👇

Not just you (Diary study: a link, not proof.)

Source: Gordon & Chen (2014), "The Role of Sleep in Interpersonal Conflict: Do Sleepless Nights Mean Worse Fights?", Social Psychological and Personality Science

title: lonely_young
caption:
Who's the loneliest age group in the world? Not your grandparents. 🫥

Gallup and Meta asked people in 142 countries how lonely they feel. Almost 1 in 4 adults said very or fairly lonely. That's more than a billion people.

The loneliest group: ages 19 to 29, at 27%. The least lonely: 65 and older, at 17%.

So if you're young and lonely, you're not the exception. You're the biggest group.

Tag someone you should call this week 👇

Not just you. (Survey, 142 countries, 2022–23.)

Source: Gallup & Meta, Global State of Social Connections (2023)

title: sex_facts
caption:
3 bedroom facts worth saving. All backed by research. 🛏️

1. Once a week is enough. In data from over 30,000 people, well-being rose with sex up to once a week. More didn't help.

2. Don't skip the cuddle. Couples who spent more time on affection after sex felt more satisfied.

3. The afterglow lasts about two days.

So: once a week. Cuddle after. Enjoy the glow.

Save this. 👇

Not just you (Facts 1 and 2 are links, not proof.)

Sources: Muise, Schimmack & Impett (2016), Social Psychological and Personality Science · Muise, Giang & Impett (2014), Archives of Sexual Behavior · Meltzer et al. (2017), "Quantifying the Sexual Afterglow", Psychological Science

title: single_men
caption:
Under thirty, there's a dating gap. And it's huge! 💔

Pew Research asked over 6,000 Americans about their love lives. Under 30, 63% of men said they're single. Women? 34%.

And among singles of all ages, 50% of the men are looking for someone. Only 35% of the women.

So if you're young, male and single, you're not behind. You're the majority.

Why do you think that is? 👇

Not just you (Survey of 6,034 US adults, July 2022. Single = not married, not living with a partner, not in a committed relationship.)

Source: Pew Research Center (2023), "For Valentine's Day, 5 facts about single Americans"

title: no_friends
caption:
15% of men have zero close friends. Back in 1990? 3%. 🫂

A national survey asked 2,019 Americans how many close friends they have. Five times as many men now have nobody.

Men with 6 or more close friends dropped from 55% to 27%. And last week, 41% of women got emotional support from a friend. Men? 21%.

So if your circle got smaller, you're not the exception. You're the trend.

How many close friends do you have? 👇

Not just you (Survey of 2,019 US adults, May 2021, compared with 1990.)

Source: Survey Center on American Life (2021), "The State of American Friendship"; 1990 vs 2021 figures for men via its director Daniel Cox

title: follower_math
caption:
Your followers are more popular than you. And that's just math! 📱

If yes, you're probably right. And it's not about you.

Researchers analyzed 5.8 million Twitter users and 476 million tweets. A typical user's followers had about 10 times more followers than the user.

And 88% of users posted less than the people they follow (99% if you leave out inactive accounts).

It's math: popular accounts follow and get followed by lots of people, so they show up in everyone's network. Including yours. It's called the friendship paradox.

So you're not boring. Your feed is just a room full of the most popular people.

Does your feed feel like this? 👇

Not just you (Platform data: Twitter, second half of 2009.)

Source: Hodas, Kooti & Lerman (2013), "Friendship Paradox Redux: Your Friends Are More Interesting Than You", ICWSM

title: couple_posts
caption:
The couples who post the most aren't always the happiest. 📸

Researchers ran three studies on how people show their relationship on Facebook, including a daily diary. On days people felt more insecure about their relationship than usual, they posted more about it.

People with anxious attachment, the ones who worry their partner might leave, wanted their relationship to be the most visible. Avoidant people did the opposite: fewer couple photos, fewer relationship statuses.

So a feed full of couple photos isn't proof of love. Sometimes it's a quiet ask for reassurance.

Do you post your partner? 👇

Not just you (3 studies, partly self-reported. A link, not a rule.)

Source: Emery, Muise, Dix & Le (2014), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

title: met_online
caption:
Most couples don't meet through friends anymore! 💘

Stanford researchers asked thousands of American couples how they met. In 1995, friends were the top matchmaker: 33%. By 2017, just 20%.

Online went from 2% to 39%. Now the most common way couples meet.

So if you met your partner on an app, you're not the weird story. You're the normal one.

How did you meet? 👇

Not just you (Surveys of straight US couples, 2009 and 2017.)

Source: Rosenfeld, Thomas & Hausen (2019), "Disintermediating your friends", PNAS

title: likes
caption:
Likes change what you like. And your brain can't help it. ❤️

UCLA researchers showed 32 teens an Instagram-style feed inside a brain scanner. The trick: the researchers set the likes themselves. Same photo, lots of likes or just a few.

With lots of likes, teens were more likely to like the photo too. Even their own photos. And the brain's reward center lit up more for the popular ones.

So you don't just like what's good. You like what's already liked.

Do you check the likes first? 👇

Not just you (Small study: 32 teens aged 13 to 18.)

Source: Sherman et al. (2016), "The Power of the Like in Adolescence", Psychological Science

title: vulva_normal
caption:
There's no such thing as a "normal" vulva. Scientists measured it. 🌸

Swiss gynecologists measured 657 women aged 15 to 84. How far the inner lips stick out: from 1 millimeter to 6 centimeters. Their length: from half a centimeter to 10.

So what's normal? All of it.

But normal doesn't mean you have to love it.

In one small experiment, women looked at photos of real vulvas. Afterwards, they felt better about their own, and still did two weeks later. Neutral photos changed nothing.

So look at real ones, like these. And if it still weighs on you, talk to a doctor.

Send this to someone who needs it. 👇

Not just you (Bodies: all normal, part 1. Measurements in one Swiss hospital. The photo experiment was small: 43 women.)

Sources: Kreklau et al. (2018), "Measurements of a 'normal vulva' in women aged 15–84", BJOG · Lloyd et al. (2005), "Female genital appearance: 'normality' unfolds", BJOG · Laan et al. (2017), "Young women's genital self-image and effects of exposure to pictures of natural vulvas", J. of Psychosomatic Obstetrics & Gynecology

title: size_normal
caption:
Most men worry about their size. Most don't need to! 📏

A review pooled 17 studies and up to 15,521 men. Measured by health professionals, not self-reported.

The average: 13.1 centimeters. About 5.2 inches.

Yet in a survey of over 50,000 people, only 55% of men were happy with their size. And 85% of women were satisfied with their partner's size.

But knowing the average doesn't make the worry go away.

In one clinic, 92 men came in worried about their size. Getting measured and learning the real numbers relieved most of them.

So if it still bothers you, talk to a doctor. That's what helped.

Send this to a friend who worries. 👇

Not just you (Bodies: all normal, part 2. The survey was online and self-selected. The clinic study was small and had no comparison group.)

Sources: Veale et al. (2015), "Am I normal?", BJU International · Lever, Frederick & Peplau (2006), "Does Size Matter?", Psychology of Men & Masculinity · Shamloul (2005), "Treatment of men complaining of short penis", Urology

title: reach_out
caption:
You lost touch with a friend. Text them today. 📲

In a series of experiments with more than 5,900 people, participants sent a short note to someone they hadn't talked to in a while.

First, they guessed how much it would be appreciated. Then the friends answered: they loved it more than the senders expected.

And the more out of the blue the message was, the bigger the gap.

So send the text. Right now. It means more than you think.

Who are you texting? 👇

Not just you (Experiments by one research team. The bars in the video show the direction, not exact values.)

Source: Liu, Rim, Min & Min (2022), "The Surprise of Reaching Out: Appreciated More Than We Think", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

title: more_sex
caption:
You think everyone is doing it more than you. They're not. 📅

Across 19 countries, people guessed how often young adults have sex: about 20 times a month. The real number: 5 to 6 times. That's what young adults themselves report.

And in couples, happiness rose with sex only up to about once a week. More didn't add more.

So stop comparing. You're probably closer to normal than you think.

Send this to someone who compares. 👇

Not just you (The "real" numbers are self-reports from national surveys. The once-a-week finding is a link, not proof, and didn't show up for singles.)

Sources: Ipsos (2018), "Perils of Perception" · Muise, Schimmack & Impett (2016), "Sexual Frequency Predicts Greater Well-Being, But More Is Not Always Better", Social Psychological and Personality Science

title: stay_leave
caption:
You've thought about breaking up. And you stayed. 🚪

Researchers followed over 1,300 people in relationships for ten weeks. Then 500 who were thinking about leaving.

So who stayed? The ones who believed their partner needed them. Even when they weren't happy themselves.

So staying often comes from caring. That's kind. Just don't forget your own needs.

Save this for a hard day. 🔖

Not just you (Two studies from one team, a link, not proof. If a relationship hurts you or you don't feel safe, please reach out to someone you trust or a local helpline.)

Source: Joel, Impett, Spielmann & MacDonald (2018), "How Interdependent Are Stay/Leave Decisions?", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

title: friend_paradox
caption:
Your friends have more friends than you. That's math, not you. 🧮

We simulated a friend group of 26 people with one very popular person: 23 of 26 had fewer friends than their friends.

Why? Picture one very popular person. Lots of people count them as a friend. So whenever people look at their friends, that person shows up again and again, and the average goes up.

A sociologist checked this in a high school: most students had fewer friends than their friends did. 55% of the girls.

So if everyone seems more social than you: that's an illusion. Not a you problem.

Send this to a friend. They have more. 👇

Not just you (The "friendship paradox" is a property of networks. The school data come from a classic study of the late 1950s, analyzed in 1991.)

Source: Feld (1991), "Why Your Friends Have More Friends Than You Do", American Journal of Sociology

title: dishes
caption:
You fight about the dishes. That's not a small thing. 🍽️

Asked what makes a good marriage, Americans said: faithfulness, 93%. Good sex, 70%. Sharing chores, 62%.

But a newer study found that splitting chores 50/50 isn't enough. What works: sharing the tasks themselves. Of couples who shared every task, 99% called it fair. Split 50/50 without sharing: only about half.

So don't just divide the chores. Do some together. Start with the dishes.

Who does the dishes? 👇

Not just you (US surveys, a link, not proof. Earlier work by the same researcher found sharing the dishes was the chore most tied to women's satisfaction.)

Sources: Pew Research Center (2007), "Modern Marriage" · Carlson (2022), Sex Roles · Carlson et al. (2018), Council on Contemporary Families

title: deep_talk
caption:
You avoid deep talks because you think they'll be awkward. They're not. 💬

In twelve experiments with more than 1,800 people, strangers were paired up. Some got small talk questions. Others got deep ones. Like: when did you last cry in front of someone?

First, they predicted how awkward it would be. Then they talked: far less awkward than expected. And the deep talks felt closer and more fun.

People also underestimated how interested the other person was in them.

So skip the weather. Ask the real question.

What's your best deep question? 👇

Not just you (Mostly strangers in the lab, one research team. The bars show the direction, not exact values.)

Source: Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2021), "Overly Shallow? Miscalibrated Expectations Create a Barrier to Deeper Conversation", Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

title: sleep_apart
caption:
You sleep better alone. About a third of people sleep apart, at least sometimes. 🛏️🛏️

In a survey of 2,000 Americans, one in five sometimes sleeps in another room because of their partner. 15% do it regularly.

And the ones who move out most often: men. 45%, versus 25% of women. Millennials most of all: 43%.

So sleeping apart isn't a breakup. Good sleep comes first. Just keep some time in bed together.

Team one bed or two? 👇

Not just you (One online survey commissioned by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. "Keep some time in bed together" is our idea, not a survey result.)

Source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2023), "Sleep Prioritization Survey"

title: new_friends
caption:
You haven't made a new friend in years. That's not you. It's your age. 📉

Researchers analyzed the calls of over 3 million phone users. How many people is each one in touch with? It peaks at 25.

After that, our circle shrinks, until it levels off in our late forties.

And a close friend takes over 200 hours together.

So it's not that you're hard to like. Life got full. Pick one person and keep showing up.

Tag the one you'll show up for. 👇

Not just you (Phone calls from one European country in 2007 – calls, not friendships. The columns in the video show the shape, not exact values.)

Sources: Bhattacharya, Ghosh, Monsivais, Dunbar & Kaski (2016), "Sex Differences in Social Focus Across the Life Cycle in Humans", Royal Society Open Science · Hall (2019), "How Many Hours Does It Take to Make a Friend?", Journal of Social and Personal Relationships

title: the_look
caption:
You catch yourself looking at her body. Your eyes got there in a fifth of a second. 👀

In an eye-tracking study, men's first look at a woman's photo landed on her chest or waist. Faster than 200 milliseconds. Before her face.

But it's not just men: asked to rate a woman's looks, both men and women looked longer at her chest and waist than at her face.

And being looked at has a cost. In an experiment, women whose bodies were stared at solved fewer math problems afterward: just under 5 of 12, versus about 6. Men's scores didn't drop.

So the first glance is fast. The stare is a choice. Look at her face.

Send this to someone who stares. 👇

Not just you (Three small studies, mostly with students and photos. Why the eyes go there – evolution, culture or both – is still debated.)

Sources: Dixson et al. (2011), Archives of Sexual Behavior · Gervais, Holland & Dodd (2013), "My Eyes Are Up Here", Sex Roles · Gervais, Vescio & Allen (2011), Psychology of Women Quarterly

title: first_move
caption:
You wait for them to text first. Here's what that costs you. 💌

Let's simulate it: ten people on each side. Everyone secretly ranks everyone. One side asks. The other side holds on to the best offer so far. Round after round, until everyone is matched.

The askers got their number two on average. The ones who waited: number five.

Swap the sides, and it flips. The math is proven: in this model, asking never makes you worse off.

In this model, asking never makes you worse off. It's a proven theorem. Real dating is messier, of course. But the lesson holds: send the first message.

Send the first message. Then save this. 🔖

Not just you (A simulation of the Gale-Shapley matching model with random rankings, not a study of real couples. The model won a Nobel Prize in 2012 for its use in matching markets.)

Sources: Gale & Shapley (1962), "College Admissions and the Stability of Marriage", American Mathematical Monthly · Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences 2012 (Roth & Shapley)

title: berkson
caption:
You think attractive people are mean. It's a statistics trick. 🎲

Let's simulate it: 400 people. Looks and kindness are totally random, no link at all.

Now you only date people who are attractive enough, kind enough, or both. Among the ones left, the better looking they are, the meaner they get.

Because the mean and plain ones never made your list. So the hot ones you meet don't need to be nice to get there.

It's called Berkson's paradox. It's not that hot people are mean. It's who you filtered out.

Send this to someone who dates jerks. 👇

Not just you (This is a simulation, a math model, not a survey. It shows how a filter alone can create a fake link.)

Sources: Berkson (1946), Biometrics Bulletin · Ellenberg (2014), "How Not to Be Wrong"

title: 37_rule
caption:
You settled too early. Or you waited too long. There's a rule for that. 🃏

Say you'll date ten people, one after another. Once you pass on someone, they're gone. So when do you commit?

The math says: skip the first 37%. Just look. Then pick the first one who beats them all.

We simulated 1,000 love lives, ten dates each. The rule found the very best one 40% of the time. Committing to the first date, or picking at random: only about 10%.

Real life is messier. People can say no, and you never know how many you'll meet. But the lesson holds: explore first. Then commit.

Too early or too late? 👇

Not just you (A simulation of the "secretary problem", a math model, not a study of real couples.)

Sources: Ferguson (1989), "Who Solved the Secretary Problem?", Statistical Science · Christian & Griffiths (2016), "Algorithms to Live By"

title: five_close
caption:
You only have room for about four close people. 📞

Researchers looked at about 6 billion phone calls between 35 million people. Who you call most forms circles:

About 4 people. Then 11. Then 30. Then about 130.

Your inner circle: about four. That's all most of us keep that close.

So losing touch with the rest isn't failing. It's a limit.

Who are your four? 👇

Not just you (Averages from call records in one European country, 2007. Calls are only a proxy for closeness. The classic estimate is 5 / 15 / 50 / 150.)

Source: MacCarron, Kaski & Dunbar (2016), "Calling Dunbar's numbers", Social Networks

title: birthday
caption:
You're in a room with 23 people. Two of them probably share a birthday. 🎂

365 days, only 23 birthdays. Sounds unlikely. So we simulated 1,000 rooms.

About half of them had a match. The math says 50.7%. With 70 people: 99.9%.

Why? 23 people make 253 pairs. Every pair is a chance.

Ever met someone with your birthday? 👇

Not just you (Simulation and math assume every day is equally likely and ignore leap years.)

Source: the birthday problem, classic probability theory

title: five_to_one
caption:
One fight with your partner needs about five good moments to balance it. ⚖️

A researcher filmed couples while they argued, then checked who was still together years later.

Couples who lasted: about 5 good moments for every bad one. Even during the fight.
Couples close to a split: 1 to 1, or less.

A joke. A touch. A nod. They add up.

What's your go-to good moment mid-argument? 👇

Not just you (Observational studies. The exact ratio is debated, and it's a pattern, not a rule for every couple.)

Source: Gottman & Levenson (1992), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology · Gottman (1994), "What Predicts Divorce?"

title: next_door
caption:
Your closest friends probably live closer than you think. 🚪

In 1950, researchers mapped friendships in a student housing block.

Next-door neighbors: 41% became friends.
Two doors away: 22%.
End of the hall: only 10%.

We don't pick friends from everyone. We pick from who we run into.

Who's your "next door" friend? 👇

Not just you (One classic housing study from 1950. Later studies found the same pattern, for example with classroom seating.)

Source: Festinger, Schachter & Back (1950), "Social Pressures in Informal Groups"

title: spotlight
caption:
You think everyone noticed your embarrassing shirt. They didn't. 👕

In a study, students had to wear a very embarrassing T-shirt into a room full of people.

The wearers guessed: about half of the room noticed (46%).
The real number: about one in four (23%).

Everyone else is busy thinking about themselves. Just like you.

What's the thing you were sure everyone noticed? 👇

Not just you (One experiment with students. Later studies found the same overestimation, the exact size varies.)

Source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

title: degrees
caption:
You're only about three and a half people away from almost anyone. 🌍

Facebook measured this in 2016, across 1.6 billion users.

The old idea: six steps between any two people.
The real average: 3.57 people in between. In the US: 3.46.

Your friend knows someone, who knows someone.

Who's the most surprising person you're connected to? 👇

Not just you (Facebook users only. The network in the video is a made-up example to show how far-away friends create shortcuts.)

Source: Bhagat et al. (2016), "Three and a half degrees of separation", Facebook Research

title: happy_spread
caption:
When your friend gets happier, you probably do too. 😊

Researchers followed almost 5,000 people for 20 years.

When a friend living nearby got happier, your chance of being happy went up by about 25%.
And it spread up to three steps: to friends of friends of friends.

Your mood travels further than you think.

Who's the friend who always lifts your mood? 👇

Not just you (Observational data, so it shows a link, not proof that happiness is "contagious". The 25% has a wide margin of error.)

Source: Fowler & Christakis (2008), BMJ, Framingham Heart Study

title: body_map
caption:
You think men and women get turned on in different places. Their body maps say no. 🗺️

704 people colored a body outline: where does a partner's touch turn you on?

Men and women drew almost the same map. Genitals first, then chest, inner thighs, lips.
Women's maps were a little bigger: 26% of the body vs 22%.

Turns out, we're more alike than we think.

Which spot surprised you? 👇

Not just you (One online study with Finnish volunteers, more women than men. Self-reported maps, not measurements.)

Source: Nummenmaa et al. (2016), "Topography of Human Erogenous Zones", Archives of Sexual Behavior

title: body_mind
caption:
Your body can react before your mind is into it. Especially for women. 🧠

Researchers combined 132 lab studies with over 4,000 people. They measured two things: what the body did, and what people said they felt.

For men, body and mind mostly moved together.
For women, much less. The body often reacted on its own.

So a body's reaction is not a yes. Only a clear yes is.

Did you know this? 👇

Not just you (Lab studies. Part of the gap comes from how arousal was measured. A body reaction says nothing about wanting or consent.)

Source: Chivers et al. (2010), Archives of Sexual Behavior, meta-analysis

title: split_all
caption:
If we split all the world's wealth equally, 9 out of 10 people would get richer. 🪙

Researchers added up what every adult on Earth owns: homes, savings, companies, minus debts.

Today the richest 10% hold about 75% of it. The poorer half shares just 2%.
Split equally, every adult would get over $100,000. That's about 20 times what the poorer half owns now.

If your stack feels small, you're in the majority.

What would you do with your equal share? 👇

Not just you (A thought experiment, not a policy. Wealth is homes, firms and land, not cash you could hand out, and prices would change. Figures in purchasing-power dollars, rounded.)

Source: World Inequality Report 2026 (World Inequality Lab); cross-check UBS Global Wealth Report 2026

title: split_income
caption:
If we split the world's income equally, people in rich countries would live on about a third. 🌍

The world produces about $26,000 per person a year (adjusted for prices).

The US and Germany sit about 3 times above that. India and Nigeria far below.
Split equally, everyone would live roughly like an average person in Mexico or Thailand today.

Rich countries would take a pay cut. Most of the world would get a raise.

Would your life get better or worse? 👇

Not just you (A thought experiment. Uses GDP per person in purchasing-power dollars, not take-home pay, and ignores how income is shared within each country. Figures rounded.)

Source: IMF World Economic Outlook 2025 (GDP per capita, PPP). Part 2 of "Split it all" (No. 136)

title: guess_wish
caption:
How much does the richest fifth own? Most people guess way too low. 🪙

5,522 Americans estimated how wealth is split, then built the split they'd wish for.

Their guess: the richest 20% own 59%.
Their wish: 32%.
The truth: 84%. The poorest 40% share less than 1%.

We picture the world fairer than it is.

What would you have guessed? 👇

Not just you (US data from the 2000s. Some people may have thought of income, not wealth. Only the top-fifth numbers are exact, the other bars are schematic.)

Source: Norton & Ariely (2011), Perspectives on Psychological Science

title: middle
caption:
Ask people where they stand, and almost everyone says: the middle. 🪜

Researchers asked over 30,000 people in 10 countries where their household ranks.

In every country, at least 2 in 3 of the poorer people placed themselves too high.
Richer people did the opposite and placed themselves too low.
Only a minority got their own step right.

If you feel pretty average, so does almost everyone.

Where would you place yourself? 👇

Not just you (Survey data, rough income fifths. The "richer people too low" part comes from a separate study in Denmark. Dots are schematic.)

Source: Hoy & Mager (2021), American Economic Journal: Economic Policy; Hvidberg, Kreiner & Stantcheva (2023), Review of Economic Studies

title: global_rich
caption:
If you take home $20,000 a year, you're richer than 9 in 10 people on Earth. 🌍

Researchers lined up everyone's income, after tax and adjusted for prices.

The person right in the middle lives on about $3,400 a year.
$20,000 puts you in the top 10%. In Germany or the US, more than half of people are there.

Feeling average at home can mean rich on Earth.

Did you expect that? 👇

Not just you (For a one-person household, after tax, in international dollars that adjust for living costs. Bars are schematic except the middle and the top-10% line.)

Source: Our World in Data (2025), based on World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform

title: black_friday
caption:
Is Black Friday really the cheapest day of the year? 🛒

A consumer group tracked 208 Black Friday deals, every day for a whole year.

Only 5 were cheapest on Black Friday itself. That's 2%.
The other 98% were just as cheap, or cheaper, on another day.

➡️ Verdict: false.

So before you buy, check the price history, not the countdown.

What are you buying this Black Friday? 👇

Not just you (UK study: 8 big retailers, Black Friday 2022, prices tracked six months before and after. Even counting the whole two weeks around Black Friday, 86% were cheaper or the same at another time.)

Source: Which? (2023), Only 2% of discounted products are cheapest on Black Friday

title: love_new
caption:
In 1967, 3 in 4 young American women wouldn't rule out marrying without love. 💍

Students were asked: would you marry someone perfect for you, if you weren't in love?

Only 24% of women said no. For most, love wasn't a must. (Among men it was 65%.)
By the 1990s, only 3.5% of Americans said yes.

Love as the main reason to marry is newer than you think.

Would you? 👇

Not just you (College students in the US, so not everyone. In 1967 many women depended on marriage for money and status, which likely shaped their answers.)

Source: Kephart (1967), Journal of Marriage and the Family; Levine et al. (1995), Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology

title: what_sells
caption:
More than half of all countries earn most of their export money from raw materials. 🛢️

Oil, metals, crops. Dug up or grown, then sold.

Oil and coal: from Norway to Nigeria to Saudi Arabia.
Gold, copper and other metals: much of Africa and the Andes.
Crops: coffee in Ethiopia, cocoa in Ivory Coast, soy in Brazil.
Cars, phones and medicine: mostly Europe and East Asia.

Most of the world still drills, digs or grows.

What does your country sell most? 👇

Not just you (The map shows each country's single biggest export in 2018, grouped into four types. One product isn't the whole economy, and services like tourism aren't included.)

Source: UNCTAD, The State of Commodity Dependence 2023; CEPII BACI trade data via Visual Capitalist

title: best_country
caption:
The best country to live in changes with every thing you count. 🌍

We compared 89 countries on five things:

☀️ Best weather: Uruguay, Malta, Portugal
🛡️ Safest: UAE, Qatar, Taiwan
🛒 Cheapest food: Pakistan, India, Iran
💰 Most buying power from a salary: Kuwait, Qatar, Switzerland
🏠 Cheapest rent: Bangladesh, Pakistan, India

A different number one every time. The best place depends on what matters to you.

Which of the five matters most to you? 👇

Not just you (Numbeo data is crowd-sourced from users, mostly city dwellers, so treat it as a rough guide. Only 89 countries have all five values.)

Source: Numbeo, Quality of Life & Cost of Living Index by Country, 2026 Mid-Year

title: affair_world
caption:
Is having an affair always wrong? Depends on where you ask. 🌍

Over 30,000 people in 25 countries were asked if it's morally unacceptable.

Indonesia and Turkey: 92% say yes.
The US: 90%.
France: 53%. Germany: 55%. Barely half.

So what counts as a dealbreaker depends a lot on where you grew up.

Where would your country land? 👇

Not just you (Survey from 2025. The other answers were "morally acceptable" or "not a moral issue". Countries in grey weren't part of the survey.)

Source: Pew Research Center (2026), 25-country survey on morality

title: japan
caption:
Japan judges an affair more mildly than its neighbors. 🇯🇵

In a 2025 survey, 65% of Japanese called an affair morally wrong.
In South Korea it was 83%. In the US, 90%.

At home, nearly half of married people in Japan had no sex in the past month.

What marriage means, and what it allows, really depends on the country.

What surprised you more? 👇

Not just you (Two different surveys. "No sex in the past month" is how the Japan Family Planning Association defines a sexless marriage. A commercial survey from 2024 even reports 64%.)

Source: Pew Research Center (2026); Japan Family Planning Association (2023 survey, via Japan Times)

title: friends_count
caption:
How many close friends is normal? Fewer than you think. 🫂

In 2021, Americans were asked to count their close friends.

Almost half have one to four.
One in eight has none.
In 1990, a third had ten or more. Now, only 13%.

If your circle feels small, you have the most common size there is.

How many do you have? 👇

Not just you (US survey from 2021, during the pandemic. The 1990 numbers come from Gallup. "Five to nine" is the rest.)

Source: Survey Center on American Life (2021); Gallup (1990)

title: middle_class
caption:
Are you middle class? Here's where the line is. 💵

Researchers call it middle income if a household earns two thirds to double the typical income.

For a family of three: about $57,000 to $170,000 a year.
Half of all US adults are inside. 28% below, 19% above.

So the middle isn't one number. It's a wide band, and most people are in it.

Where do you land? 👇

Not just you (US data for 2022. The band changes with household size and local prices. Pew has a calculator for your exact case.)

Source: Pew Research Center (2024), The State of the American Middle Class

title: bank_normal
caption:
How much money does a normal American under 35 have in the bank? 🏦

The Federal Reserve checked: checking, savings, the lot.

The average: about $20,500.
But the person in the middle has just $5,400.
A few big accounts pull the average up.

So if your account looks small next to the average, compare it to the middle instead.

Where do you stand? 👇

Not just you (Per household, by age of the head of household, 2022. Doesn't include retirement accounts or investments. Bars are schematic.)

Source: Federal Reserve, Survey of Consumer Finances 2022

title: happy_age
caption:
Life satisfaction falls until your late forties. Then it climbs back. 📈

Over 4,000 adults in Scotland rated their life from 0 to 10.

Early twenties: 8.1
Around fifty: 7.5
Late sixties: back up to 7.9

Across 132 countries, the low point is around age 48.
The dip is small, but real.

So if midlife feels heavy, you're right on schedule. And it tends to lift.

Where are you on the curve? 👇

Not just you (These are averages across different age groups, not the same people over time. Some long-term studies find a weaker dip or none at all.)

Source: Scottish Health Survey 2016; Blanchflower (2021), Journal of Population Economics

title: cheat_line
caption:
Is flirting cheating? Fewer than half of Americans say yes. 🤔

2,000 adults rated what counts as cheating in a marriage.

A secret emotional bond: 76% say cheating.
Flirting: 42%.
Following an ex online: 32%.
Secret porn: 30%.

So if you and your partner draw the line in different places, that's normal.

Where's your line? 👇

Not just you (One US survey from 2019. "Secret porn" means without the partner knowing. Worth talking about before it matters.)

Source: iFidelity Survey (YouGov 2019, Wheatley Institution & National Marriage Project), via Institute for Family Studies

title: birthday
caption:
How many people need to be in a room for a 50/50 chance that two share a birthday? 🎂

Lock in your answer before the reveal. 👀

The real answer: just 23.

Why? Everyone gets compared with everyone. 23 people make 253 pairs, and every pair is a chance for a match.
At 70 people, a match is almost certain (99.9%).

If you guessed way higher, your gut counted people, not pairs.

What did you guess? 👇

Not just you (Math with 365 equally likely birthdays, no leap day, no twins. Real birthdays are slightly uneven, which makes a match a little more likely.)

Source: The birthday problem, standard probability (e.g. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory)

title: humanity_island
caption:
Give every human alive one square meter. How much land do we need? 🌍

Lock in your answer before the reveal. 👀

8.2 billion people × 1 m² = 8,200 km².
That's Crete (8,336 km²). All of humanity fits on one Greek island, just barely.

Earth has about 18,000 times more land than that.

Space isn't the problem. Food, water and energy are.

What did you guess? 👇

Not just you (1 m² per person standing, not living space. World population mid-2026 ≈ 8.2 billion.)

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, International Database (2026); Crete area 8,336 km²

title: life_england
caption:
How long did people in England live? Here are 475 years. ⏳

1541: 38 years.
1558: 14 years (a flu epidemic).
1665: 23 years (the Great Plague).
For three centuries, it hovered around forty.

Then, in about 150 years, it doubled: 41 in 1870, 81 today.

Not because old people got older, but because children stopped dying.

Which year surprised you most? 👇

Not just you (Life expectancy at birth. The low numbers were driven mostly by infant and child deaths. Adults who made it through childhood often lived into their 60s. Early centuries: England estimates.)

Source: Gapminder, UN, IHME via Our World in Data (life expectancy at birth, United Kingdom, 1541–2016)

title: murder_europe
caption:
How violent was medieval Europe? Here are 700 years of murder rates. 🗡️

Italy around 1300–1450: 56 to 73 killings per 100,000 people, every year.
Then, century by century, it kept falling.
Today: below 1. About 60 times lower.

Germany & Switzerland: 37 → 0.8. England: 23 → 0.5.

Your ancestors didn't just live shorter lives. They lived far more dangerous ones.

Which century would you have survived? 👇

Not just you (Historical rates are estimates from court and coroner records for selected regions, so they're rough. But every region shows the same long decline.)

Source: Eisner (2003), Long-Term Historical Trends in Violent Crime; IHME (from 1990), via Our World in Data

title: gold_cube
caption:
All the gold in the world, melted into one cube. How big is it? 🪙

Lock in your answer before the reveal. 👀

224,200 tonnes: every ring, coin and bar ever made.
It's a cube about 23 meters wide. As tall as a seven-story building.
Thousands of years of gold rushes, standing on two tennis courts.
Worth about 30 trillion dollars.

Gold isn't valuable because there's a lot of it. It's valuable because there's so little.

What did you guess? 👇

Not just you (Above-ground stocks end of Q3 2026, rounded. The value moves with the gold price.)

Source: World Gold Council, How much gold has been mined? (2026)

title: farm_per_person
caption:
How much farmland does it take to feed one person? Guess the size. 🌾

Lock in your answer before the reveal. 👀

All the farmland on Earth, split evenly: about 5,900 m² each.
Almost a whole football pitch.

80% of it feeds animals: pasture and feed crops.
But that part gives us only 17% of our calories.

Most of the field feeds animals. The small corner feeds most of us.

Did you guess bigger or smaller? 👇

Not just you (Global averages. Animal products give 17% of calories but 38% of protein. 4% of farmland grows non-food crops like cotton and biofuels.)

Source: Our World in Data (2024), based on UN FAO and Poore & Nemecek (2018)

title: price_of_light
caption:
How expensive was light? Here are 700 years of prices in England. 🕯️

In 1300, light cost over 10,000 times more than today.
For five hundred years, the price barely moved.
Then came gas lamps, kerosene and the light bulb.

1300: £33,000 per million lumen-hours. 2006: under £3. (In 2000 pounds, inflation-adjusted.)

For most of history, darkness was the cheap option.

Would you have gone to bed at sunset? 👇

Not just you (A million lumen-hours is roughly one bright bulb running for 1,250 hours. The price is the average across candles, oil, gas and electricity.)

Source: Fouquet & Pearson (2006), Seven Centuries of Energy Services, via Our World in Data

title: child_mortality
caption:
How many children died before their fifth birthday? The whole world, since 1800. 👶

1800: 43 out of 100.
1900: still more than 1 in 3.
Then came vaccines, clean water and antibiotics.
Today: about 4 out of 100.

That's the real reason life expectancy doubled.

Did you know it was this high? 👇

Not just you (Historical numbers before 1950 are estimates. 4 out of 100 is still millions of children a year, mostly from preventable causes.)

Source: Gapminder and World Bank (2019), via Our World in Data

title: height_germany
caption:
How tall were German men 200 years ago? Here's every generation. 📏

Born around 1850: 1.64 m on average.
Then, generation by generation, they grew.
Born in 1980: 1.80 m. 17 cm taller.

Same genes. Better food, cleaner water and fewer childhood illnesses.

How much taller are you than your grandparents? 👇

Not just you (Men only, by year of birth. Historical data comes from soldiers and conscripts, so it's an estimate.)

Source: University of Tübingen, Baten & Blum (2015), Human Height, via Our World in Data

title: literacy
caption:
How many people in the world could read? Here's every decade since 1820. 📖

1820: 12 out of 100.
1950: just over half.
Today: 86 out of 100.

That you can read this was, for most of history, a rare privilege.

Who taught you to read? 👇

Not just you (Adults 15+. Historical values are estimates, and "literate" was measured differently over time. Around 750 million adults still can't read today.)

Source: Our World in Data, based on OECD (2014) and UNESCO

title: wild_vs_farm
caption:
All the wild land mammals on Earth, against all the farm animals. Which pile weighs more? 🐘🐄

Lock in your answer before the reveal. 👀

Elephants, deer, wolves and mice: about 20 million tonnes.
Cows, pigs and sheep: about 630 million tonnes.
Farm animals weigh 30 times more.

All wild land mammals together: about 2.5 kg per person.

By weight, most mammals on Earth now live on farms.

Did you guess right? 👇

Not just you (Weight = total body mass. Wild marine mammals like whales add about 40 million tonnes, still far below livestock.)

Source: Greenspoon et al. (2023), The global biomass of wild mammals, PNAS

title: light_doku
caption:
The year is 1800. Night falls, and Mary wants her room as bright as yours, for just one hour. 🕯️

That one hour of light will cost her almost six hours of work.
Her light comes from tallow candles, made of animal fat. To make a room as bright as yours, she would need about 80 of them, burning all at once.

For five hundred years, the price of light barely moved. So for most people, the day simply ended at sunset.
Then, in less than a century: gas lamps, kerosene and the light bulb.

Today, the same hour of light costs you less than half a second of work.

What would you do with six extra hours of evening? 👇

Not just you (Mary is illustrative. "As bright as yours" = 1,000 lumen-hours, about one modern bulb for an hour. Labour times are economist William Nordhaus' estimates.)

Source: Nordhaus (1996), The History of Lighting; Fouquet & Pearson (2006), via Our World in Data. Pictures: Wikimedia Commons (public domain, CC0; candle makers' workshop: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: no_smile
caption:
Paris, 1838. A busy boulevard: carriages, horses, people everywhere. But in the very first photo of it, the street is empty. 📷

The picture needed minutes of light. Everything that moved simply vanished. Except one man, standing still to get his boots shined.

That's how you got into a photo: you froze. Studios even put iron stands behind your head. Blink, and your face became a blur.
By the 1850s it took just a few seconds. People still didn't smile: a photo was rare, expensive and forever. Some were even told to say "prunes" to keep the mouth small.

Then, in 1900, Kodak's Brownie camera cost one dollar. Suddenly everyone took snapshots, and the smile moved in.
Today, your phone takes a photo in less than a hundredth of a second.

Would you have smiled for a photo that lasts forever? 👇

Not just you (The street film is from 1897 and only illustrates a busy Paris street. The exposure time of Daguerre's 1838 photo is estimated at several minutes.)

Source: J. Paul Getty Museum (2023), "Say Prunes!"; Daguerre, Boulevard du Temple (1838); Kodak/George Eastman Museum. Pictures and film: Wikimedia Commons, Internet Archive (public domain)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: wash_day
caption:
Monday, 1900. Anna gets up before dawn. Today is wash day, and it will take her the whole day. 🧺

One load of laundry needs about 50 gallons of water. Every drop, carried in by hand.
She hauls it from the pump, heats it on the stove, scrubs every shirt on a washboard, boils it, wrings it, hangs it out.
In one year she walks about 150 miles just carrying water. That's 36 tons.

And the work isn't over: Tuesday is ironing day, with heavy irons heated on that same stove.
Then came running water, electricity and the washing machine.

Today you press one button, and you don't even have to watch.

What would you do with your Mondays back? 👇

Not just you (Anna is illustrative, the numbers are for an American household around 1900. The washerwomen film is from France, 1897.)

Source: Susan Strasser (1982), Never Done: A History of American Housework, via Digital History, University of Houston. Pictures and film: Wikimedia Commons, Internet Archive (public domain)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: two_weeks
caption:
London, 1763. The person you love lives in Edinburgh, and you want to see them. 💌

The coach takes two weeks, and it only leaves once a month.
Four hundred miles of muddy roads, horses changed again and again, and every night you stop at an inn.

In 1784, John Palmer had an idea: put the mail on fast coaches, with fresh horses at every stage and a guard with a gun.
By 1830, mail coaches ran day and night. London to Edinburgh in under two days.
Then came the railway, the telegraph and the phone.

Today, your message arrives before you put the phone down.

Who would you travel two weeks for? 👇

Not just you (The lovers are illustrative. The train film is American, 1897.)

Source: All the Year Round (Dickens' magazine), vol. VI; The Spectator, 11 July 1829, "The North Mail"; The Postal Museum (UK). Pictures and film: Wikimedia Commons, Internet Archive (public domain)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: ice_ship
caption:
May 1833. A ship leaves Boston for India. Its cargo: 180 tons of ice. 🧊

Four months at sea, straight across the equator.
The man behind it was Frederic Tudor. Years earlier, people had laughed at him. A Boston paper joked about a "slippery speculation".
His ice was cut from frozen lakes in New England, packed in sawdust and stacked tight, so it would melt slowly.

When the ship reached Calcutta, more than half was still frozen: 100 tons.
People in India drank ice-cold drinks from American lakes, and Tudor became known as the Ice King.

Today, your freezer makes ice in a few hours, right in your kitchen.

Would you have bet on shipping ice across the world? 👇

Not just you (The harbour film is from 1897 and only illustrates a ship leaving port. The newspaper line is from 1806, about Tudor's first ice cargo to Martinique.)

Source: American Heritage, "Cold Mine"; Smithsonian Magazine; Atlas Obscura. Pictures and film: Wikimedia Commons, Internet Archive (public domain)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: cowpox
caption:
England, 1796. A doctor takes pus from a milkmaid's hand and scratches it into the arm of an 8-year-old boy. 💉

Weeks later, he infects the same boy with smallpox. On purpose.
Smallpox killed about three in ten people who caught it. Many survivors were scarred, or blind.

The doctor was Edward Jenner. He had heard that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, never got smallpox.
Would it work? The boy, James Phipps, never got sick.

People were scared. A famous 1802 cartoon showed vaccinated people growing cows. But the name stuck: vaccination, from "vacca", Latin for cow.
In 1980, smallpox was declared gone, the only human disease ever eradicated.

It all started with one boy, one milkmaid and a cow named Blossom. 🐄

Did you know where the word vaccine comes from? 👇

Not just you (Infecting a child on purpose would never be allowed today. Blossom's hide still hangs in a London medical school library.)

Source: WHO, "History of smallpox vaccination"; Jenner (1798), An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae; Gillray (1802), "The Cow-Pock". Pictures: Wikimedia Commons, Wellcome Collection (public domain, CC BY 4.0)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: love_match
caption:
London, 1743. A wedding is being arranged, and the bride and groom barely look at each other. 💍

Because they didn't choose. Their parents did.
In Hogarth's famous painting, an earl points at his family tree and a rich merchant brings the money. Love isn't part of the deal.

For most of history, marriage was about land, money and alliances. Love was thought far too fragile to build a life on.
But about 200 years ago, a radical idea spread: marry for love. Balls, letters, courtship.
Then came dating, divorce and finally the apps.

Today, about 8 in 10 people say they're looking for a soulmate.

Would you have let your parents pick? 👇

Not just you (The soulmate figure is from US surveys. The ball film is from 1897.)

Source: Stephanie Coontz (2005), Marriage, a History: From Obedience to Intimacy, or How Love Conquered Marriage; Hogarth, Marriage A-la-Mode (c. 1743). Pictures and film: Wikimedia Commons, Internet Archive (public domain)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: merer
caption:
2013. In caves by the Red Sea, archaeologists find something they never expected: papyrus, rolled up and covered in writing. 📜

It's a diary, written by a man who helped build the Great Pyramid.

For centuries, people asked how the pyramid was even possible. Some said: aliens.
The diary's author was Merer, an inspector who led about 40 boatmen and wrote down their days, one by one.
What he wrote is no mystery: load stone at Tura, sail the Nile, unload at Giza. About 30 blocks per trip, around 200 a month.
The stone was white limestone, most likely for the pyramid's smooth outer shell.

It's the oldest inscribed papyrus ever found in Egypt, over 4,500 years old.

No aliens. Just a diary, and forty men on a boat.

What do you think is still unexplained about the pyramids? 👇

Not just you (The papyrus shown is a similar ancient letter, used for illustration. The alien idea is a popular claim with no evidence behind it.)

Source: Pierre Tallet (2017), Les papyrus de la Mer Rouge I; Tallet & Marouard (2014), Near Eastern Archaeology; National Geographic. Pictures: Wikimedia Commons, The Met, Rijksmuseum (public domain, CC0). Satellite maps: Sentinel-2 cloudless 2016 by EOX, CC BY 4.0
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: antikythera
caption:
In 1901, sponge divers pulled a lump of bronze from a 2,000-year-old shipwreck. ⚙️

A year later, someone spotted a gear inside it. A tiny, hand-cut gear.
Nothing that complex would be built for another thousand years. Some said: aliens.

But X-ray scans revealed more than 30 bronze gears and tiny Greek writing.
Turn a handle, and it tracked the sun and the moon, and predicted eclipses.

Today, scientists call it the oldest known analog computer.

No aliens. Just a lump of bronze, and Greek genius.

Which ancient mystery should we solve next? 👇

Not just you (It's called the Antikythera mechanism and is in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. Built around 150–100 BC.)

Source: Freeth et al. (2006), Nature 444; Linda Hall Library. Pictures: Wikimedia Commons (CC0, CC BY)

title: mary_celeste
caption:
December 4, 1872. A ship drifts across the Atlantic, sails up, and nobody is on board. 🚢

Ten people gone: Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife Sarah, their 2-year-old daughter Sophia and seven crew.
The ship could still sail. Six months of food. Their things still there.
But the lifeboat was gone, one pump was taken apart, and there was water in the hold.

The newspapers wrote "pirates". Others blamed mutiny, a sea monster, even something from the sky. A young Arthur Conan Doyle wrote a made-up story about it, and many readers believed it.
A court in Gibraltar found no sign of a crime.

The most likely idea: Briggs feared the ship was sinking or the alcohol might explode, and took everyone into the lifeboat. It was never found.

What do you think happened? 👇

Not just you (The newspaper clipping is real: Boston Post, February 24, 1873.)

Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica; Smithsonian Magazine; Boston Post (1873). Pictures: Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
Voice: Kyutai Pocket TTS (alba), CC BY 4.0

title: middle
caption:
Ask people where they stand, rich or poor, and almost everyone says the same thing: the middle. 🪜

Two economists asked over 30,000 people in 10 countries, from Nigeria to the UK: where does your household rank?

In every country, at least 2 in 3 of the poorer people placed themselves too high. In Nigeria, more than 9 in 10.
In Denmark, where answers were checked against tax records, richer people placed themselves too low.
Only a few got their own step right.

If you feel pretty average, so does almost everyone.

Where would you place yourself? 👇

Not just you (Survey data, rough income fifths. The "richer people too low" part comes from a separate study in Denmark. Dots are schematic.)

Source: Hoy & Mager (2021), "Why Are Relatively Poor People Not More Supportive of Redistribution?", American Economic Journal: Economic Policy; Hvidberg, Kreiner & Stantcheva (2023), Review of Economic Studies
